title: Plate work
subtitle: Flat metal ribbon bent in zigzags across a padded shape for a highly reflective filling
excerpt: Plate work uses a flat, mirror-bright metal strip bent back and forth across a raised shape, each turn couched to hold it in place. The flat surface of the metal reflects light across the whole area with far more intensity than a woven or couched thread surface.
sourceNotes: Barbara Dawson, Metal Thread Embroidery (1968), plate work chapter. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), plate and or nué entries. Royal School of Needlework standard goldwork curriculum.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat, highly polished metal strip, wider than passing thread. It cannot be taken through the fabric and is bent in zigzags across the surface, held at each turn by a couching stitch.

Lengths of string or cotton cord couched flat in the shape of the design area and then covered by the goldwork. The raised profile increases light reflection from metal threads and plates laid over it.

content.text: Plate work gives a goldwork design a mirror-like brilliance that no other metal thread technique can match. Metal
plate

is a thin, flat metal ribbon, wider than a passing thread, with a highly polished surface. Because it cannot be threaded through fabric, it is bent in close zigzags across the shape and couched at each turn. A layer of
string padding
or felt beneath the plate raises the surface and increases the angle of reflection, making the finished area appear to glow.
What you need

items.label: Metal thread
items.value: Gold or silver plate, 2 to 3 mm wide; handle with tweezers or clean dry cloth to avoid tarnishing

items.label: Couching thread
items.value: One strand of waxed gold or yellow silk, pulled through beeswax before use

items.label: Ground
items.value: Firm silk or linen mounted on a slate frame; string padding or several layers of felt couched inside the design shape beforehand

items.label: Needle
items.value: Fine sharps needle size 10 for couching; mellor or laying tool for easing the plate flat

content.text: Working the stitch

Build the padding first. Couch down string or cord inside the outline of the shape, following its contour. Add a second layer across the first at right angles, then a third if a high profile is needed. Alternatively, cut felt to the shape outline in graduated sizes and stack them, couching each layer flat.
Thread the fine needle with a single waxed strand of silk. Bring it up at one edge of the padded shape.

Lay a length of plate across the shape from one side to the other, keeping it flat and untwisted. Use tweezers or a mellor to position it. Make a couching stitch over the plate at the edge of the shape, pulling it snug to hold the plate down at the turn without scoring or kinking it.
Bend the plate back to cross the shape in the opposite direction, placing it immediately against the previous row with no gap between the two strips. Couch at the opposite edge.

Continue across the shape, bending and couching at each edge. All the bends should fall just outside the design outline so the couching stitches at the turns are hidden by the pearl purl or other outline thread that is added last.

When the shape is filled, cut the plate at the last turn and neaten the end with a couching stitch. Apply pearl purl or another outline thread around the edge to cover the turns and give a clean finish.
Common mistakes

items.symptom: The plate twists and the rows show a dull side rather than the polished face
items.cause: The plate rotated at the bend instead of folding cleanly.
items.fix: Hold the plate firmly with tweezers at the turn and fold it with a thumbnail or the flat of the mellor rather than bending it freehand. The fold should be a clean crease, not a twist.

items.symptom: The plate surface shows fingerprint marks and tarnish
items.cause: Handling the plate directly with bare hands.
items.fix: Always handle plate with tweezers or with a clean dry cloth between your fingers and the metal. The oils in skin begin to tarnish the surface immediately.

items.symptom: Gaps between rows make the ground fabric visible
items.cause: Each row was not placed immediately against the last.
items.fix: After laying each strip, slide it against the previous one using the mellor before making the couching stitch at the edge.

content.text: Uses and related stitches
Plate work appears most often in heraldic goldwork and church embroidery, where it fills small shapes such as shields or crowns that need intense reflection. It is finished with a
couching
outline and pairs well with
or nué
areas in the same design.
